title: Gas laws
categories: Changes of state and thermal expansion

questions.prompt: Which quantity describes thermal energy transferred because of a temperature difference?
questions.explanation: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because their temperatures differ.

questions.prompt: Which is a unit of heat transferred?
questions.explanation: Heat is an energy transfer, so it is measured in joules. Kelvin and Celsius measure temperature.

questions.prompt: For an ideal gas, a higher Kelvin temperature means a higher average…
options: number of particles in every container
questions.explanation: Kelvin temperature is proportional to the mean translational kinetic energy of ideal-gas particles.

questions.prompt: Thermal energy transfers spontaneously between two touching bodies in which direction?
options: From lower temperature to higher temperature
Always from the larger object to the smaller
Always from the denser object to the less dense
From higher temperature to lower temperature
questions.explanation: The temperature difference determines the spontaneous direction of heat transfer.

questions.prompt: Convert 27°C to Kelvin using 273.15.
Convert 300 K to Celsius.
Which change doubles absolute temperature?
questions.explanation: Only Kelvin ratios describe changes in absolute temperature. 20°C to 40°C is about 293 K to 313 K, not a doubling.

questions.prompt: Absolute zero corresponds to which temperature?
questions.explanation: Absolute zero is the lower limit of thermodynamic temperature, not the freezing point of water.

questions.prompt: An ideal gas is heated from 200 K to 400 K. What happens to its mean translational kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Mean translational kinetic energy is proportional to Kelvin temperature.

questions.prompt: Which statement about extrapolating gas graphs toward 0 K is most accurate?
options: A real gas can be cooled to negative Kelvin temperatures by simple cooling
It is an ideal-model extrapolation; a real gas may condense before reaching very low temperatures
Every gas stays gaseous all the way to 0 K
0 K means every material has no internal energy of any kind
questions.explanation: Real gases can depart from the ideal-gas model, especially near changes of state. A backwards line is not a measurement made at 0 K.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: What is the change from liquid to gas at the surface of a liquid called?
questions.explanation: Evaporation occurs at the surface and can happen below the boiling point.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes boiling from evaporation?
options: Only evaporation changes a liquid into a gas
Evaporation requires bubbles throughout the liquid
Boiling forms vapour bubbles throughout the liquid; evaporation occurs at its surface
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature for the prevailing pressure.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: What is condensation?
questions.explanation: Cooling water vapour can lead to condensation into liquid droplets.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: Dry ice changes directly from solid to gas. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is a direct solid-to-gas change.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: At ordinary atmospheric pressure of about 101 kPa, pure water boils at approximately…
questions.explanation: Water boils at about 100°C near standard atmospheric pressure. Its boiling temperature changes when pressure changes.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: During the melting plateau of a pure substance heated steadily at constant pressure, why does temperature remain nearly constant?
options: The sample loses all its mass
Energy is used in the phase change rather than raising the mean kinetic energy
questions.explanation: During the phase change, supplied energy changes the arrangement/interactions of particles instead of raising temperature.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: A cooling curve has a flat section while a pure gas becomes liquid at constant pressure. Which change is occurring?
questions.explanation: Gas and liquid may coexist while energy leaves during condensation.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: Which statement best describes thermal expansion?
options: Expansion always means a chemical reaction
Particle separations usually increase; the particles themselves do not simply swell
Every particle becomes a larger particle
questions.explanation: Heating can increase average particle separation. The individual molecules do not expand like balloons.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: A sealed balloon is cooled while outside pressure stays approximately constant. What usually happens to its volume?
options: It doubles whatever the temperature change
questions.explanation: Cooling lowers Kelvin temperature; a flexible gas container can contract. A balloon is only approximate because its rubber affects pressure.

questions.category: Changes of state and thermal expansion
questions.prompt: Which point is essential when comparing melting or boiling temperatures?
options: Assume boiling points never depend on pressure
Ignore the identity of the substance
State the external pressure and whether the substance is pure
questions.explanation: Changes-of-state temperatures depend on substance, purity and pressure.

questions.prompt: Pressure is defined as…
questions.explanation: P = F/A: pressure is force per unit area.

questions.prompt: One pascal is equivalent to…
questions.explanation: The SI pressure unit is the pascal, one newton per square metre.

questions.prompt: For the same force, halving the contact area makes the pressure…
questions.explanation: P = F/A; pressure increases when the same force acts over less area.

questions.prompt: Why do skis help distribute a skier’s weight on soft snow?
options: They increase pressure by reducing area
Their larger contact area reduces pressure
questions.explanation: For the same weight, a larger supporting area means lower pressure.

questions.prompt: A force of 500 N acts over 20 cm². What is the pressure in N/cm²?
questions.explanation: 500 ÷ 20 = 25 N/cm². This is the worked pressure example in the presentation.

questions.prompt: A force of 600 N acts over 0.03 m². What pressure is produced?
Convert 125,000 Pa to kPa.
questions.explanation: Divide pascals by 1000 to obtain kilopascals.

questions.prompt: Convert 2.5 dm³ to cm³.
questions.explanation: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so 2.5 dm³ = 2500 cm³.

questions.prompt: Which pair describes the STP convention used in your presentation?
questions.explanation: This course uses 0°C (273.15 K) and 100 kPa as its standard reference.

questions.prompt: A tyre gauge measures pressure above atmospheric pressure. What pressure is used in gas-law ratios?
options: Only the gauge reading in every calculation
questions.explanation: Gas-law equations require absolute pressure. Gauge pressure is relative to the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Which condition must be constant for Boyle–Mariotte’s law, besides the amount of gas?
questions.explanation: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume.

questions.prompt: At fixed temperature, a sealed sample is compressed from 100 mL to 50 mL. Its pressure…
questions.explanation: Halving volume doubles pressure because PV remains constant.

questions.prompt: Why does compressing a sealed sample at constant temperature increase pressure?
options: Particles collide with the walls more frequently in the smaller space
questions.explanation: The same particles have less space. At fixed temperature, mean kinetic energy stays constant.

questions.prompt: Which equation expresses Boyle–Mariotte’s law?
questions.explanation: The product of absolute pressure and gas volume is constant when temperature and amount are fixed.

questions.prompt: A gas occupies 100 cm³ at 100,000 Pa. It is compressed to 80 cm³ at constant temperature. Find its final pressure.
A fixed gas sample occupies 4.00 dm³ at 210 kPa. What pressure gives 2.50 dm³ at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: P₂ = 210 × 4.00/2.50 = 336 kPa, matching the presentation example.

questions.prompt: If pressure rises from 100 kPa to 400 kPa at constant temperature, an initial volume of 8 L becomes…
questions.explanation: Pressure becomes four times larger, so volume becomes one-quarter as large.

questions.prompt: What does a graph of pressure against volume look like for Boyle–Mariotte’s law?
options: A curve that increases as volume increases
A straight line through the origin with positive slope
A horizontal line for every volume
questions.explanation: P is proportional to 1/V, so the P–V relationship is an inverse curve.

questions.prompt: Which graph is linear through the origin for an ideal Boyle–Mariotte experiment?
options: Pressure against Celsius temperature with changing amount
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives P = constant × (1/V).

questions.prompt: Which procedure better approximates a constant-temperature syringe experiment?
options: Compress rapidly and assume temperature cannot change
Add more gas during each reading
Keep the plunger fixed while heating
Compress slowly so thermal energy can be exchanged with the surroundings
questions.explanation: Rapid compression can heat gas; slow changes allow closer thermal equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Charles’s law links which two quantities at fixed pressure and fixed gas amount?
questions.explanation: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature when pressure is constant.

questions.prompt: Which apparatus best represents Charles’s law?
options: A sealed syringe whose volume is forcibly fixed
A gas cylinder with a freely moving piston under a fixed load
A completely rigid sealed vessel that is heated
An open empty beaker with gas freely escaping
questions.explanation: The piston can move so that gas pressure balances a constant external load.

questions.prompt: A gas at constant pressure is warmed from 300 K to 600 K. What happens to its volume?
options: It becomes four times as large
questions.explanation: V/T remains constant, so doubling Kelvin temperature doubles volume.

questions.prompt: A gas has volume 22 L at 280 K. At the same pressure, what is its volume at 320 K, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: V₂ = 22 × 320/280 = 25.142… L, which rounds to 25.1 L.

questions.prompt: A gas occupies 2.32 dm³ at 40°C. It is heated to 75°C at constant pressure. What is its final volume, approximately?
Why is using 20°C to 40°C as a doubling in Charles’s law incorrect?
options: Volume never changes when gas is heated
The ratio must use absolute Kelvin temperatures
Celsius and Kelvin increments have different sizes
questions.explanation: 20°C and 40°C correspond to 293.15 K and 313.15 K, not a factor of two.

questions.prompt: A gas occupies 3 L at 300 K. What volume is predicted at 200 K with pressure constant?
On a graph of volume against Kelvin temperature at fixed pressure, the ideal relationship is…
options: a straight line with negative slope
a straight line extrapolating through the origin
questions.explanation: V is directly proportional to T in the ideal-gas model.

questions.prompt: Which gas property stays constant as a loaded piston moves outward in a Charles experiment?
options: The total number of gas particles must double
questions.explanation: Volume increases so the pressure can continue balancing the fixed external load.

questions.prompt: Why is an ordinary balloon only an approximate Charles-law model?
options: Its gas temperature can never change
Its rubber membrane changes the pressure as it stretches
It must always be a rigid container
questions.explanation: Membrane tension affects internal pressure; a fixed-load piston is a closer constant-pressure model.

questions.prompt: Which conditions are fixed in the pressure–temperature law?
questions.explanation: For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, P is proportional to Kelvin T.

questions.prompt: Two identical sealed 2 L cylinders contain the same amount of gas at 400 K and 800 K. Which has greater pressure?
options: The 800 K cylinder has zero pressure
questions.explanation: The temperature doubles at fixed volume and amount, so pressure doubles.

questions.prompt: How do particles explain higher pressure when a rigid sealed container is heated?
options: They move faster and transfer more momentum in more frequent wall collisions
questions.explanation: Heating raises mean kinetic energy; wall collisions create the pressure.

questions.prompt: Which equation represents the constant-volume pressure law?
questions.explanation: Pressure divided by Kelvin temperature stays constant for a fixed gas amount and volume.

questions.prompt: A rigid tank contains gas at 3.20 atm and 22°C. At 60°C, its pressure is approximately…
A rigid container holds gas at 100 kPa and 300 K. What pressure is predicted at 450 K?
At fixed volume, a gas is cooled from 400 K to 200 K. What happens to its pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure changes in the same ratio as Kelvin temperature.

questions.prompt: Which graph is expected for pressure against Kelvin temperature at constant volume?
options: A straight line extrapolating through the origin
questions.explanation: Absolute pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature.

questions.prompt: If the pressure–Celsius-temperature line is extended backwards in the ideal model, where does zero pressure occur?
questions.explanation: The Celsius-axis intercept corresponds to 0 K; it is an ideal-model extrapolation, not a real zero-pressure measurement.

questions.prompt: Why can heating affect pressure differently in a rigid tank and a freely moving piston?
options: The gas has no mass inside a tank
The piston changes Kelvin into Celsius
Pressure can only exist in a rigid tank
The tank fixes volume; the loaded piston allows volume to change at approximately fixed pressure
questions.explanation: The constraint determines whether thermal expansion appears mainly as changing volume or changing pressure.

questions.prompt: Which quantity must remain fixed when applying the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂?
questions.explanation: The combined law compares states of the same amount of ideal gas.

questions.prompt: Gas at 110 kPa, 30°C and 2.0 dm³ is changed to 440 kPa and 80°C. What is the new volume, approximately?
For a fixed gas amount, both pressure and Kelvin temperature double. What happens to volume?
questions.explanation: From PV/T = constant, V is proportional to T/P, so equal doubling factors cancel.

questions.prompt: A fixed gas sample doubles its volume while its Kelvin temperature stays fixed. Which change is required?
questions.explanation: The combined law reduces to Boyle–Mariotte when temperature is fixed.

questions.prompt: When using the combined gas law, what is essential about the units in the two states?
options: Use consistent pressure/volume units and Kelvin temperatures
Use kPa in one state and Pa in the other without conversion
Use litres in one state and cm³ in the other without conversion
questions.explanation: Matching units allow like quantities to form meaningful ratios.

questions.prompt: Which equation is the ideal gas equation?
questions.explanation: P is absolute pressure, V volume, n amount in moles, R the gas constant and T Kelvin temperature.

questions.prompt: Which unit combination is consistent with R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹?
options: P in Pa, V in dm³ and T in °C
P in atm, V in cm³ and T in K without converting R
P in kPa, V in dm³ and T in K
P in kPa, V in cm³ and T in °C
questions.explanation: 1 kPa·dm³ = 1 J. Pa with m³ and Kelvin is also consistent.

questions.prompt: Using PV = nRT, estimate n for gas at 200 kPa in 10 dm³ at 300 K, with R = 8.31.
Convert 0.025 m³ to dm³ before using kPa with R = 8.31.
An ideal gas has n = 0.50 mol, T = 300 K and P = 100 kPa. Find V using R = 8.31.
Equal volumes of ideal gases at the same pressure and temperature contain equal…
questions.explanation: This is Avogadro’s principle. Different gases can have different masses per particle.

questions.prompt: At fixed pressure and temperature, doubling the amount of ideal gas makes its volume…
questions.explanation: Avogadro’s law gives V proportional to n when P and T are fixed.

questions.prompt: At the course STP of 273.15 K and 100 kPa, one mole of an ideal gas occupies approximately…
questions.explanation: This convention gives a molar volume of about 22.7 dm³/mol; the standard pressure must be specified.

questions.prompt: At STP (273.15 K and 100 kPa), what volume does 5 mol of ideal carbon dioxide occupy?
questions.explanation: V = n × molar volume = 5 × 22.7 = 113.5 dm³.

questions.prompt: At STP (273.15 K and 100 kPa), how many moles are in 45.4 dm³ of an ideal gas?
questions.explanation: n = volume/molar volume = 45.4/22.7 = 2.0 mol.

questions.prompt: Equal volumes of oxygen and nitrogen are at the same P and T. Which statement is correct?
options: Oxygen must contain more molecules because it is heavier
Nitrogen must contain more molecules because it is lighter
They contain equal numbers of molecules, but need not have equal masses
questions.explanation: Equal gas volumes at equal P and T have equal particle numbers; molecular masses can differ.

questions.prompt: What does n represent in PV = nRT?
questions.explanation: n is amount of substance measured in moles.

questions.prompt: Why must pressure and temperature be stated when giving the volume of one mole of gas?
options: Only the container colour determines the volume
Gas volume changes when pressure or temperature changes
A mole has a different number of particles every day
All gases always occupy 22.7 dm³ whatever the conditions
questions.explanation: Molar volume depends on the specified conditions, even for ideal gases.

questions.prompt: At STP (273.15 K and 100 kPa), 0.25 mol of ideal gas occupies approximately…
A sealed gas sample is heated without a leak or chemical reaction. What happens to its amount in moles?
questions.explanation: Heating changes energy and may change pressure or volume; it does not by itself change the number of gas particles.
